interviewQuestions.question: Why can't we write a program that detects infinite loops in general?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd connect this directly to the halting problem rather than treating it as a separate question: "does this loop ever terminate" for an arbitrary program is exactly an instance of "does this program halt on this input."

I'd sketch the impossibility argument at a high level: assume a perfect loop-detector `H` exists. Build a program `D` that asks `H` about itself and then deliberately does the opposite of what `H` predicts — if `H` says "halts," `D` loops forever instead, and vice versa. Either answer `H` gives about `D` running on itself turns out wrong, so no such `H` can exist.

I'd close with the practical angle: this is exactly why real tools (linters, static analyzers) don't try to solve the general case — they use conservative heuristics, correctly flag common patterns (bounded counters, obvious recursion without a base case), and explicitly say "can't determine" rather than claim false certainty on adversarial or complex code.

**Testing:** whether you can connect a concrete engineering question to the underlying undecidability result, and explain the proof idea, not just cite "halting problem" as a buzzword.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Connecting infinite-loop detection to the halting problem

interviewQuestions.question: Why do we treat the Turing machine as *the* model of computation, when it's just one specific design among many possible machine models?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The Turing machine isn't privileged because it's realistic hardware — it's an intentionally minimal, almost crude model (an infinite tape, a single read/write head, a finite set of states). It's privileged because of the **Church-Turing thesis**: every other reasonable model of computation anyone has proposed — lambda calculus, register machines, cellular automata, real programming languages, quantum computers restricted to classical-equivalent tasks — has been proven to compute exactly the same set of functions, no more and no less. Nobody has ever found a genuinely different, more powerful notion of 'effectively computable' that isn't equivalent to a Turing machine.

This convergence is why 'undecidable for a Turing machine' is treated as 'undecidable, period' rather than 'undecidable for this one specific quirky machine' — the halting problem's unsolvability isn't an artifact of the tape-and-head design, it would show up in essentially any model you invented, because they're all equivalent in what they can compute (Turing-completeness), even though they differ enormously in *convenience* and *efficiency* for expressing a given algorithm.

The practical takeaway that follows directly: when someone says a language or system is 'Turing-complete' (regex-with-backreferences, CSS with certain hacks, even Magic: The Gathering's rules have been shown Turing-complete), that's a real, meaningful claim about its computational ceiling — it can compute anything any computer can, in principle, even though it would be a terrible tool to actually write software in. Turing-completeness is about *capability*, not *practicality*.

**Testing:** whether you understand the Church-Turing thesis as the reason the model generalizes (not an arbitrary historical choice), and can apply the Turing-complete label correctly to unconventional systems.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Church-Turing thesis

interviewQuestions.question: Beyond the halting problem itself, how do you prove a *different* problem — like 'does this function ever return null' — is also undecidable?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The standard technique is **reduction**, structurally identical to how NP-hardness proofs work but pointed at undecidability instead of intractability: show that if you *had* a hypothetical decider for the new problem, you could use it to build a decider for the halting problem (or another already-known-undecidable problem) — since the halting problem has no decider, neither can the new one.

Concretely, for 'does this function ever return null': given an arbitrary program `P` and input `x` (the halting problem's inputs), construct a new function `f` that runs `P` on `x`, and only returns `null` if `P` halts (otherwise `f` loops forever or returns something else). If a decider for 'does f ever return null' existed, running it on this constructed `f` would tell you whether `P` halts on `x` — solving the halting problem. Since that's impossible, no such decider for 'returns null' can exist either.

This reduction pattern is formalized by **Rice's theorem**, which says almost *any* non-trivial semantic property of a program's behavior (not syntactic properties like 'does the source contain a for-loop,' but behavioral ones like 'does it always terminate,' 'does it ever throw,' 'is it equivalent to this other program') is undecidable in general — which is precisely why static analysis tools for real languages always have some combination of false positives, false negatives, or an explicit 'cannot determine' escape hatch: they're not failing to try hard enough, they're up against a proven mathematical wall, and the honest engineering response is heuristics with known, documented blind spots, not a false promise of completeness.

**Testing:** whether you can execute a reduction-style undecidability proof concretely, and whether you know Rice's theorem as the general principle behind why so many real program-analysis questions turn out undecidable.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Reductions and Rice's theorem

interviewQuestions.question: If the halting problem is provably undecidable, why do static type checkers and linters still catch real bugs — aren't they trying to solve exactly this?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
They don't attempt the general, unrestricted problem — they deliberately trade completeness for decidability by restricting either the property they check or the language of programs they check it over, and being explicit about that trade is exactly what makes them work.

A type checker doesn't ask 'will this expression ever produce a runtime type error on any possible execution' in full generality (undecidable) — it asks a more conservative, structurally-checkable question: 'does this program pass the type system's specific, decidable set of rules,' which is deliberately designed to be **sound but incomplete** — every program the checker accepts genuinely is type-safe (sound), but some programs that would actually run fine get rejected anyway because the checker's rules aren't smart enough to see why they're safe (incomplete). That's a conscious design trade-off, not a limitation anyone is trying to hide — language designers choose exactly how much expressiveness to sacrifice for decidability.

The general engineering pattern this represents, seen across static analysis, terminates-detection heuristics, and linters alike: undecidability doesn't mean 'give up,' it means 'you cannot build a tool that's simultaneously sound, complete, and terminates on every possible program' — so every real tool picks two of those three. A linter that flags 'possible infinite loop' heuristically is complete-ish and terminates but isn't sound (false positives); a formally verified subset language sacrifices generality (some programs simply can't be written in it) to get soundness, completeness, and termination together. Recognizing which corner of that trade-off a given tool occupies is exactly the senior-level version of this question.

**Testing:** whether you can name the specific trade-off (soundness vs completeness vs generality) each real tool makes, rather than treating 'undecidable, but tools still work somehow' as a contradiction.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Real-world undecidability
